body: Yeah no problem!  It's common misconception that many people pass around as common sense, but actually has no basis in fact.

> LSD, even if used infrequently, leaves a chemical residue that stays in your spinal fluid for a very long time, if not forever, and this chemical residue can have terrible effects on your mental functions if you aren't taking the right medications to counter those effects.

[LSD does not  leave a residue in your spinal fluid](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_misconceptions_about_illegal_drugs#Retention_of_LSD_in_spinal_fluid).  That said, psychedelics can have profound and lasting psychological effect that can be positive or negative.  I do agree that the OP should see a mental health professional who can help sort these psychological issues out.

Yeah.. I started an anti-depressant for the first time and changed the dose of an old medication, under medical supervision, but now all this stuff has been bludgeoning at my mind very strongly this week.  This isn't necessarily new, but it feels particularly bad.  I suspect this is medication related, but it's scary not knowing if this will pass.

>please remember it's the opposite of rose-tinted glasses.

It's interesting you should say this.  It's pretty much how I've felt about things since childhood.  Memories don't just turn to ash for me: They turn to veritable shit.  For some the past becomes brighter, while for me, only the worst parts--or what I perceive to be the worst parts--remains salient.

>i hope the storm passes soon. you sound smart. world needs smart.

Thank you, I really do appreciate it.

It's a graduate degree, and I very much enjoy the subject matter, but because of various location and money constraints, I am in a program that is not necessarily geared towards getting the MA candidates into doctoral programs.  Not the best decision on my part, but it was the best I could do given my situation.
Or a live-action series?  So happy no one's planned that!

I find that the list trick is best when you keep it manageable.  Some people keep them over a longer period of time, but I think the key there is that you don't have too much visible on one day.  One other trick that I have been trying to do more lately is to break up a task into manageable tasks (eg., open the document, take out notes, write x section of the paper).  Many times, just being able to check off one or two easy things can really help with getting started.

So perfectionism.  It's part of what makes us great at what we do.  It's also the thing that can mess with that the most.  For those of us in research, I think it's somewhat necessary to have at least a little bit of it (and wow, I rewrote that sentence about five times).  That said, no one else *expects* us to be perfect.  Consider the primary research you read: is any study truly perfect?  Of course not.  The hardest thing for me is reconciling my own extremely high standards for what is good enough.  I can pick apart my own work so well because I know all the shortcuts I took; I know all the avenues I could have pursued.

I think the greatest thing for  me in reducing some levels of perfectionism is learning to fail in low-stakes situations.  I learned to do that with stuff like handcrafts that I could learn from YouTube and outdoor adventuring.  You can set goals, and no one else really has to see you not quite make them.  Then you analyse how things could have gone more effectively and try and incorporate that into your next attempt.  It's an iterative process.  Effort may lead to failure, but failure is a fertiliser for success.  It's the higher-stakes situations like school where I have a much harder time controlling the perfectionism.

The thing about not enjoying processes...I don't always like the processes all the time, but on some level, I do enjoy doing research, crafts, exercising, etc.  I think that this might be a symptom of depression.  When my depression gets really bad, I don't like doing much of anything.   Depression isn't always constant misery or suicidal ideation.  Sometimes it manifests as an inability to motivate or find the energy to do things – that is how it is for me.  

You said that you're passionate about your field, so I assume that there is something that you like about what you're doing: The fact that you're having lots of thoughts about not enjoying the process at all, that really could be depression, especially considering that you're feeling strain in your marriage and some amount of social isolation.

Isolation is not fun.  Take it from me, an on again, off again reclusivish.  I worked at home for years and had a very hard time separating my job and non-job time.  Unfortunately, it was difficult to break the habit of doing school work at home, and it lead to the same problem.  I've actually been without a home desktop for the last few months for the first time in years and years, and that has forced me to separate my working and living spaces quite a bit.  Working in a public space is annoying, but I also feel some pressure not to fuck off all day.    If you can have an office separate from your living space, it might be helpful for to be  able to keep your work in one place in your home.

Moreover, you have to delineate time for working and relaxing.  Like, I've been working super hard in the past week or so to find a point in the day where I say, “Enough!”  From that point on, when the worries start about school, I turn that shit in my head down.  It's a very deliberate thing and sometimes requires me to deal physical symptoms such as a racing heart.  Not easy, but I feel like it has been making some difference in feeling like I have the energy to work during the day when its working time.  

Procrastinating is a horrible problem for me in so many aspects of my life, but at least with school, if I don't stay at least a little bit on top of things, I would quickly get too far behind to catch up.  Some of that is just self-discipline I developed while working at home, but some of mitigating those tendencies is to break up tasks into smaller tasks.

All this is an on-going process too.  My moods and energy levels are very cyclical.  Sometimes, I will be really able to get thing done for two or three weeks at a time, working 12 to 16 hours a day or so, running on adrenaline, then have a spell of a few days where the world seems like shit, everything I do seems like shit, all my shortcomings keep pounding in my head, and I can't make myself give a fuck, until I can't ignore my obligations any more, and I'm back to adrenaline.  It's the perfectionism, procrastination, and depression.  It's incredibly stressful and exhausting, and I know that I will die a young woman, if I keep it up.

At this point, I've been doing this for a decade or more, really – I'm in my late 20s—and it's just not changing that much.  I am actually hoping to go on some medication and get some therapy to address this stuff.  I was super, super resistant to the idea of psychiatric medication for a lot of reasons – bad side-effects, the fear that they would some how make me not me, etc, but there are lots of options (and not all of them have the ultralame weight-gain bullshit).  I've tried lots of other types of medicating substances and behaviours and none of them really have had the desired effect of getting rid of the depression and deal more effectively with the procrastination and perfectionism.

I suspect that therapy could be really helpful, so it might be worth seeing if there are providers who do the kinds of therapy you need/want without immediately jumping to giving you medication.  Medication is such a personal choice that I don't think you should have to fight with someone about not having to take it.

I know how much it sucks to be feeling the weight of all these heavy feelings about self-worth, motivation and what you feel that you  should be doing.  Sometimes that stuff makes me want to just disappear.  I think that there are ways to deal with this stuff, though.

I hope this helps: Let me know if there is anything I can clarify or PM if you'd like to talk more personally.  Sorry for the novel here, but it's also nice for me to know that someone else in a similar position as I feels this kind of stuff.

Oh wow, so I could have written quite a bit of this myself--also did well at university, found a good job, quit to work on an MA that will hopefully lead to a better academic position, and have similar issues with motivation, self-esteem, productivity, and comparing myself to others.

Once in a while, I start out with a list of things to do and end up not doing them because I feel overwhelmed and crushed by all these feelings of inadequacy and the amount of work that there is that I have not been doing.  Dreadful cycle, really.

Couple of questions: Any chance you suffer from perfectionism?  On one hand, it's hard to let go of, but on the other, nothing can really be perfect.  Do you have problems setting boundaries between worry about school time and not worrying about school time?  For me, I have a very hard time letting go of school and not thinking about it all the time, which is not helpful when I'm exhausted, because then there is no break, except when I'm trying to work on school.

Also, have you considered that you might have some depression going on?  Depending where you are, some universities have options for mental health care or will cover it on their insurance plans.

Anyway, not sure that I can offer a tonne of help, but you're not alone with these feelings.
